source_text: Nunc, si nomen Christi, ut sportulam furunculus, cap-; tauit, cur etiam Iesus uoluit appellari, non tam expectabili; apud Iudaeos nomine? nec enim, si nos, per dei gratiam intellectum consecuti sacramentorum eius, hoc quoque nomen agnoscimus Christo destinatum, ideo et Iudaeis, quibus adempta : est sapientia, nota erit res. denique ad hodiernum Christum\' sperant, non Iesum, et Heliam potius interpretantur Christum quam Iesum. qui ergo et in eo nomine uenit, in quo Christus \' non praesumebatur? potuit in eo solo nomine uenisse, quod solum praesumebatur. ceterum cum duo miscuit, speratum et insperatum, expugnatur utrumque consilium eius. siue enim \' ideo Christus, ut interim quasi creatoris inreperet, obstrepit Iesus, quia non sperabatur Iesus in Christo creatoris, siue (ideo Iesus,) ut alterius haberetur, non sinit Christus, quia non alterius sperabatur Christus quam creatoris. quid horum \' constare possit, ignoro. constabit autem utrumque in Christo I creatoris, in quo inuenitur etiam Iesus. quomodo, inquis? : disce et hic cum partiariis erroris tui, Iudaeis. cum successor I Moysi destinaretur Auses, filius Naue, transfertur certe de pristino nomine et incipit uocari Iesus. certe, inquis. hanc prius dicimus figuram futuri fuisse. nam quia Iesus Christus\' secundum populum — quod sumus nos, nati in saeculi desertis - introducturus erat in terram promissionis melle et lacte, manantem, — id est (in) uitae aeternae possessionem, qua nihil dulcius — idque non per Moysen, id est non per legis disciplinam, sed per Iesum, (id est) per euangelii gratiam, prouenire habebat, circumcisis nobis petrina acie, id est Christi (praeceptis.) — petra enim Christus — ideo is uir, qui in huius sacramenti imagines parabatur, etiam nominis dominici inauguratus est figura, Iesus cognominatus. hoc nomen ipse Christus suum iam tunc esse testatus est, cum ad Moysen loquebatur. quis enim loquebatur, nisi spiritus creatoris, qui est Christus? cum ergo mandato diceret populo: ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam. qui te custodiat in uia et introducat in terram, quam paraui tibi; intendite illi et exaudite eum, ne inobaudieritis eum; non enim celabit te, quoniam nomen meum super illum est, angelum quidem eum dixit ob magnitudinem uirtutum, quas erat editurus, et ob officium prophetae, nuntiantis scilicet diuinam uoluntatem, Iesum autem ob nominis sui futuri sacramentum. id enim nomen suum confirmauit, quod ipse ei indiderat, quia non angelum nec Ausen, sed legum eum iusserat exinde uocitari. ergo si utrumque nomen competit in Christum creatoris, tanto utrumque non competit in Christum non creatoris, sicut nec reliquus ordo. facienda est denique iam hinc inter nos certa ista et iusta praescriptio et utrique parti necessaria, qua determinatum sit nihil omnino commune esse debere alterius dei Christo cum Christo creatoris. nam et a nobis proinde diuersitas defendenda est, sicut a nobis repugnanda est, quia nec uos probare poteritis alterius dei uenisse Christum, nisi eum longe alium demonstraueritis a Christo creatoris, nec nos eum creatoris uindicare, nisi talem eum ostenderimus, qualis constituitur a creatore. de nominibus iam, obduximus: mihi uindico Christum, mihi defendo Iesum.I
pass_a_gloss: Now, if he captured the name of Christ, like a thief a purse, why did he also wish to be called Jesus, not so much a name expected among the Jews? For even if we, through the grace of God, having attained the understanding of his sacraments, also recognize this name as destined for Christ, it does not follow that it will be known to the Jews, to whom wisdom has been taken away. Finally, they hope for Christ until this day, not Jesus, and they interpret Elijah rather than Jesus as Christ. Who, then, came in that name in which Christ was not presumed? He could have come in that name alone which was presumed. Nevertheless, since he mixed two things, the hoped-for and the unhoped-for, both plans are overthrown. For whether he is Christ, so that he might meanwhile find the creator's, Jesus contradicts, because Jesus was not hoped for in the creator's Christ, or whether he is Jesus, so that he might be considered another's, Christ does not allow, because Christ was not hoped for as another's except the creator's. I do not know which of these can be established. However, both will be established in the Christ of the creator, in whom Jesus is also found. How, you ask? Learn even from the partakers of your error, the Jews. When Joshua, the son of Nun, was destined to be the successor of Moses, he was certainly transferred from his former name and began to be called Jesus. Certainly, you say. We say that this was a figure of the future. For since Jesus Christ, according to the people - which we are, born in the deserts of the world - was to introduce into the land of promise, flowing with milk and honey, that is, into the possession of eternal life, which is sweeter than nothing - and this was not to happen through Moses, that is, not through the discipline of the law, but through Jesus, that is, through the grace of the gospel, with us circumcised by the rock of Christ, for the rock is Christ - therefore, the man who was being prepared in the images of this sacrament was also inaugurated with the figure of the Lord's name, called Jesus. Christ himself testified that this name was his, even then, when he spoke to Moses. For who was speaking, if not the Spirit of the creator, who is Christ? When, therefore, he said to the people by command: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will guard you on the way and introduce you into the land which I have prepared for you; attend to him and obey him, lest you disobey him; for my name is upon him, he called him an angel, indeed, because of the greatness of the virtues which he was to exhibit, and because of the office of a prophet, announcing the divine will, but Jesus because of the future sacrament of his name. For he confirmed his name, which he had imposed upon him, because he had commanded him to be called not angel nor Joshua, but Jesus. Therefore, if both names belong to the Christ of the creator, then neither name belongs to the Christ not of the creator, just like the rest of the order. Finally, a certain and just prescription must be made between us from now on, which determines that nothing at all should be common to the Christ of another god and the Christ of the creator. For we must defend the diversity, just as we must repel it, because you cannot prove that the Christ of another god came, unless you demonstrate that he is far different from the Christ of the creator, nor can we vindicate the Christ of the creator, unless we show him to be such as is established by the creator. We have already discussed the names: I vindicate Christ for myself, I defend Jesus for myself.

pass_b_english: If Marcion stole the name Christ like a pickpocket lifting a purse, why did he also insist on being called Jesus—a name the Jews never expected? Even though we, by God's grace, have grasped the mystery of his sacraments and recognize that this name, too, was destined for Christ, that does not mean the Jews will recognize it; wisdom has been taken from them. To this day they wait for a Christ, not a Jesus, and they read Elijah as the Christ rather than Jesus. So who came in a name where Christ was not presumed? He could have come in the one name that was presumed. Instead he mixed the hoped-for and the unhoped-for, and both strategies collapse. If he claims to be Christ so he can meanwhile track down the Creator, the name Jesus contradicts him, because Jesus was never expected in the Creator's Christ. If he claims to be Jesus so he can belong to another god, the name Christ refuses him, because Christ was never hoped for as another's except the Creator's. I cannot say which of these alternatives holds up. But both will hold up in the Christ of the Creator, in whom Jesus is also found. "How?" you ask. Learn it even from the sharers in your error, the Jews. When Joshua son of Nun was appointed to succeed Moses, he was stripped of his old name and began to be called Jesus. "Granted," you say. We said earlier this was a figure of what was to come. Since Jesus Christ was to lead the people—that is us, born in the world's desert—into the promised land flowing with milk and honey, that is, into possession of eternal life, which is sweeter than anything—and this was to happen not through Moses, that is, not through the discipline of the Law, but through Jesus, that is, through the grace of the gospel, with us circumcised by the rock of Christ, for the rock is Christ (1 Cor 10:4)—therefore the man who was being prepared as a living image of this sacrament was also inaugurated with the figure of the Lord's name, surnamed Jesus. Christ himself testified that this name was his own even then, when he spoke to Moses. Who was speaking, if not the Spirit of the Creator, who is Christ? So when he commanded the people: "Behold, I send my angel before your face to guard you on the way and bring you into the land I have prepared for you; pay attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him" (Exod 23:20-21), he called him angel because of the magnitude of the virtues he would display and because of the prophet's office, announcing the divine will, but he called him Jesus because of the future sacrament of his name. For he confirmed the name he had imposed on him, since he had commanded that he be called not angel nor Joshua, but Jesus. Therefore, if both names belong to the Christ of the Creator, then neither name belongs to a Christ who is not of the Creator, just like the rest of the arrangement. Finally, a fixed and just boundary must be drawn between us from now on, determining that nothing whatsoever should be common to the Christ of another god and the Christ of the Creator. For we must defend the distinction just as we must repel the confusion, because you cannot prove that the Christ of another god came unless you demonstrate him to be utterly different from the Christ of the Creator, nor can we vindicate the Christ of the Creator unless we show him to be exactly as the Creator constituted him. On the names we have already closed the case: I claim Christ for myself, I defend Jesus for myself.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the names Christ and Jesus, the distinction between the Creator and the 'other god' of Marcion, and the typological connection to Joshua. Scripture citations (1 Cor 10:4 and Exod 23:20-21) were correctly added to the translation to identify the allusions in the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin.
